summary: The note describes the revival of heritage grains and legumes in regional cooking, driven by interest in sustainable agriculture, crop diversity and distinctive flavors. It covers the resilience of ancient grains, the role of chefs, bakers, technology, global organizations and education, and the link between farmers, chefs and consumers. It argues the revival is a movement toward more sustainable and connected food systems rather than a passing trend.
one_line: Heritage grains and legumes are being revived by farmers, chefs, educators and technology to promote flavor, biodiversity and sustainable food systems.
key_facts: Heritage grains such as einkorn, spelt, and teff have been cultivated for thousands of years and thrive in specific regional climates and soils.
Ryan Harrison, a fourth-generation farmer from California, started reintroducing red fife wheat on his land in October 2023.
Ancient grains have deep root systems that help prevent soil erosion and improve soil health, unlike the shallow roots of many commercial crops.
Chef Maria Lopez opened a farm-to-table restaurant in Asheville, North Carolina, in December 2023, featuring Christmas Lima beans and farro.
Artisan bakers are swapping conventional flours for ones milled from ancient grains, promoting richer taste and a higher nutritional profile.
Amelia Simmons, an organic farmer in the Pacific Northwest, uses advances in organic pest control to protect crops without harmful chemicals.
Drones and satellite imagery help farmers monitor fields and optimize irrigation, supporting heritage grains that might otherwise be too labor-intensive to grow at scale.
The International Conference on Crop Diversity was held in Berlin on September 9, 2023, where leaders stressed a broader genetic base in crops for food security.
The Global Heritage Grain Alliance was established in late 2023 by international farmers and researchers to connect local efforts and share resources, knowledge, and seeds.
A grassroots organization in Portland, Oregon, launched a program in January 2024 teaching school children to grow and cook with heritage legumes; its director is Henry Clarkson.
University agricultural programs research improving yield and disease resistance of heritage grains without losing their unique qualities.
Examples of consumer availability include Ethiopian restaurants serving injera made with teff and Italian eateries serving spelt pasta.
